title: When you can't pray
hookLine: the tradition allows dry days; saying the words can bring the heart after

lines: WHY SAY IT IF I DON'T FEEL IT?
cards: Some mornings the words are just words. You open the book, you say the lines, and nothing happens inside. No warmth, no presence, no meaning.
Grief can do it. Exhaustion can do it. Sometimes it's nothing you can name: a dry season that lasts weeks.
Some who pray every day describe these stretches, and the worry that comes with them: why say it if I don't feel it? The Jewish tradition gives an answer, in two words.

teach.b: The answer is: say them anyway. Not because feeling doesn't matter. The Talmud calls prayer avodah shebalev, the service of the heart.
The heart is the point. But the tradition is realistic about how hearts work.
A medieval book called Sefer HaChinukh, explaining why the Torah gives so many physical commandments, puts it in one phrase: acharei ha-pe'ulot nimshachim ha-levavot.
After the actions, the hearts are drawn. You don't wait to feel generous before you give; you give, and generosity grows.
The Talmud says something close about learning and good deeds: keep doing them even when your motives aren't pure, because from doing it not for its own sake, you come to do it for its own sake.
The prayer book even builds the problem into the Amidah.
The verse said just before it begins, which we met weeks ago, is a request for the words themselves: "O Lord, open Thou my lips; and my mouth shall declare Thy praise."
Before you praise, you admit you need help just to start. So on a dry day, the words aren't a performance.
They're a path kept open, like walking the trail to the well even in a drought, so you still know the way when the rain comes.
And that's one reason the prayers are said together. On the days you can't carry the words, the people around you are carrying them. On another day, you'll carry them for someone else.

how: Observant Jews say the fixed prayers on schedule whether or not they feel moved, trusting that the practice and the community carry them through dry stretches; teachers encourage adding feeling where possible without waiting for it.

games.why: after the actions, the hearts are drawn: the words keep the path open until the feeling returns.

practice: Choose a short line you know, from the prayer book, like the Shema's first verse or open Thou my lips, or one that has meant something to you before. Say it slowly, out loud, five or six times, without demanding to feel anything.
If nothing shifts, that's fine; you kept the path open.
